strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant gap: existing representation alignment work is almost entirely pairwise, leading to O(M^2) scaling and no guarantee of cycle consistency when M≥3 models are involved. The paper clearly articulates why a shared 'universe' factorization is preferable.

The empirical evaluation is broad, spanning probing/stitching (CIFAR-100), clustering (MASSIVE), multilingual retrieval (TED-Multi), cross-camera re-identification (Market-1501), and cross-modal retrieval (Flickr8k), which gives reasonable evidence that the proposed GCPA method is useful across diverse settings and modalities.

The 'weak-link healing' experiment (Section 4.2.1/Fig. 2) and the incremental-addition experiment (Section 4.2.2/Fig. 3) are creative, targeted demonstrations of the practical benefits of a shared universe (stabilizing poor pairwise correspondences, and cheaply extending the universe to new models), going beyond simply reporting aggregate retrieval numbers.

The theoretical treatment of GCCA as a trace-minimization/spectral problem (Theorem B.1 and corollaries) and the consensus-agreement identity (Proposition 3.2) provide some formal grounding for the proposed correction step, connecting per-sample consensus maximization to global pairwise agreement.

The paper includes several forms of robustness/sensitivity analysis (correspondence noise stress test in Section 4.5, hyperparameter sweeps for (τ, λ) in Appendix C), which strengthens confidence that the method is not narrowly tuned to one setting.
weaknesses: The central claim that GCPA 'retains the practical benefits of the shared Procrustes frame' (i.e., preserves geometry useful for stitching) is never directly validated: the stitching/probing experiments in Section 4.2 only compare PW, GPA-ADD, and GPA-REFIT, and never report GCPA's stitching/probing accuracy. Geometric fidelity of GCPA is only assessed indirectly via an angular 'drift' metric in Appendix C.2, which is not itself validated against a downstream stitching or probing task, leaving the core trade-off claim only partially supported.

The GCPA correction mechanism (a shared MLP trained to match a per-sample consensus direction under a trust-region penalty) is fairly heuristic; unlike the GPA and GCCA formulations, it lacks a closed-form or globally optimal characterization, and no theoretical guarantee is given that the trust-penalty formulation actually achieves a principled trade-off between the GCCA and GPA optima, beyond the observation in Proposition 3.2 that increasing per-view agreement to a consensus increases total pairwise agreement (a fairly generic identity).

In the weak-correspondence stress test (Appendix A.1, Fig. 8), GCPA is shown to sometimes underperform GPA and even become unstable for small/poorly matched universes, indicating that the method is not uniformly beneficial and that its behavior under weak or noisy correspondences is not fully characterized or theoretically explained beyond a qualitative discussion.

The clustering experiment (Section 4.3) shows the odd result that GPA and GCCA barely differ from no-alignment baselines (NA) on ARI/NMI, which is surprising given that both methods are designed to align representations; this counter-intuitive result is not explained in depth, raising questions about whether the clustering protocol or metric is appropriately sensitive to the type of alignment being tested.

No comparisons are made against more expressive alignment baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., functional/spectral alignment methods such as Fumero et al. 2024, or Cannistraci et al.), which would help contextualize how much of GCPA's improvement stems from the multi-way universe formulation versus more general nonlinear alignment capacity.

Reported retrieval results (Tables 2, 3, Figures 4, 6, 7) generally lack confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing, apart from the clustering results in Table 1; this makes it harder to assess whether the (sometimes modest) margins between GCPA and GCCA/GPA are robust rather than due to noise in the correspondence sets or random initialization of Tθ.

Key implementation details for GCPA's correction network (architecture, training schedule, sensitivity to initialization) are relegated to brief appendix descriptions, and the specific values of the fixed (τ, λ) used for the 'dataset-agnostic' configuration are not clearly stated in the main text, limiting exact reproducibility without consulting the provided code.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: extending representation alignment from the pairwise setting to M≥3 models via a shared 'universe,' which reduces map complexity from O(M^2) to O(M) and enforces cycle consistency by construction.

Very broad empirical evaluation spanning probing/stitching (CIFAR-100), clustering (MASSIVE, 10 multilingual models), cross-lingual retrieval (TED-MULTI), cross-camera re-identification (MARKET-1501), and cross-modal retrieval (FLICKR8K/30K), with consistent trends across domains supporting the central GPA-vs-GCCA tradeoff and GCPA's improvement.

Extensive and honest ablation studies: sensitivity to hyperparameters (τ, λ), robustness to correspondence noise and test-time feature perturbation, incremental/continual model addition, computational cost analysis, and a 'weak-consensus' failure case where GCPA is shown to underperform GPA, which is a commendable transparent limitation.

The identity in Proposition 3.2 and the closed-form GCCA solution (Theorem B.1) give some formal grounding connecting the consensus-based correction to the sum of pairwise agreements, clarifying the intuition behind why nudging toward the mean direction increases cross-space agreement.

Clear practical utility: the ability to add new models cheaply (GPA-ADD near GPA-REFIT) and to 'heal' weak pairwise links by routing through a multi-model universe is a nice demonstrated use case with direct relevance to model merging/decentralized learning settings.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is modest: GPA is a classical technique (Gower, 1975; Schönemann, 1966) applied essentially off-the-shelf, GCCA is likewise a well-established multiset method, and GCPA itself is a fairly ad hoc post-hoc correction (a small MLP trained with a cosine-consensus loss and a trust-region penalty) rather than a principled, theoretically justified algorithm; Theorem B.1 restates known GCCA optimality results without directly justifying GCPA's own optimality or convergence properties.

No comparisons against genuinely competitive/SOTA methods in each application domain (e.g., established multilingual sentence retrieval models, supervised or state-of-the-art person re-ID cross-camera methods, or existing alignment techniques mentioned in related work such as Relative Representations or Latent Functional Maps); all comparisons are confined to the paper's own baseline family (NA/PW/GPA/GCCA/GCPA), making it hard to judge true significance of the reported gains.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: architecture, training details (optimizer, learning rate, epochs, MLP size) for the GCPA correction network Tθ are not specified in the main text and appear largely absent from the appendix, and the 'fixed dataset-agnostic' (τ, λ) values are never explicitly reported, limiting exact reproducibility.

Some results undercut the narrative without full resolution: GPA fails to improve clustering at all over no alignment (Table 1), and GCPA can underperform GPA when the multi-model consensus is unreliable (Appendix A.1/C7), suggesting the method's benefits are fairly context-dependent and the underlying mechanism for when/why correction helps vs. hurts is only empirically characterized, not theoretically predicted.

Statistical rigor is uneven: variance/seed analysis is reported only for GCPA (Appendix A.7) and not for GCCA or GPA baselines in the main results tables, so it is unclear whether reported margins (e.g., in Tables 1–3) are robust to baseline stochasticity as well.

The retrieval numbers in some settings (e.g., person re-ID mAP, multilingual rank-1) are substantially below typical benchmarks reported elsewhere in the literature for related tasks, and the paper does not contextualize why (e.g., zero-shot camera-level translation without direct image correspondence, weak base encoders), which could give an inflated impression of the practical retrieval performance achieved.
